steps.title: Putting lessons 29 and 30 together
steps.html:
Three ways of attaching information to a noun. A full relative clause (the grain that is grown in the Andes), a reduced one (the grain grown in the Andes), and a participle clause attached to the whole sentence (People were suspicious of them, thinking they were dangerous). All three are common in written English; the third is the one that goes wrong most often.

When a relative clause can be reduced. Only when the noun you are describing is the subject of that clause. The grain that is grown → the grain grown. But the foods that the Europeans introduced cannot be shortened to a participle: the clause has its own subject. You may still drop the pronoun, because it is the object: the foods the Europeans introduced.

Active or passive. The -ing form means the noun does the action (the people living there); the -ed form means the action is done to it (a grain grown in the Andes). Getting this backwards produces the grain growing in the Andes by farmers, which nobody can parse.

Commas travel with the meaning. Reducing a clause does not change whether it defines or adds: quinoa, now sold everywhere, keeps its commas; a grain grown in the Andes takes none.

Which to choose. Reduced clauses make a text denser and are normal in reports and articles. Full clauses are clearer when the sentence is already long, and are safer in speech, where a listener cannot go back.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• Reducing a clause that has its own subject: the foods introduced the Europeans.
  • Active for passive: a grain growing in the Andes by farmers.
  • Half-reduced: the people who living there.
  • Losing the commas of a non-defining clause when reducing it.
  • A participle whose subject is not the subject of the main clause.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
Beshbarmak is a dish made with boiled meat and flat squares of dough, served on one wide plate and eaten with the hands. It is what appears when there is something to celebrate, and nobody in my family thinks of it as anything but ancient.

Most of it is. The horse or lamb, the broth and the dough belong to a way of life measured in animals rather than fields. What is newer is the onion, which arrived from the west, and the potato that has quietly appeared in about half the versions I have eaten, introduced barely two centuries ago and now treated as though it had always been there.

The tea afterwards is the part guests are least aware of. Tea reached the steppe by caravan, and the sugar served with it travelled further still. A table that looks entirely local is in fact dependent on three long trade routes, only one of which anybody talks about.

Two hundred years ago the same meal would have been meat, dough, broth and salt, with no potato, less tea and no sugar at all. Whether that is preferable to what we eat now is a matter of taste. What is certain is that dishes described as traditional are usually a photograph of one particular century.
